scenes.visual: Same COLOUR MAP as the first film (16:9, warm off-white background, flat cartoon style, no molecular structures): the SIZE LADDER is a tall vertical scale on the left third of the screen, rungs labelled 0.1 µm, 1 µm, 10 µm, 100 µm, 1,000 µm = 1 mm, 10 mm, each rung ten times the one below (log spacing, evenly spaced rungs). The EYE LINE is a thick BLUE horizontal line across the ladder at 100 µm, labelled 'eye line, 100 µm'. Cells are simple cartoon icons, always the same colour: frog egg = BROWN ball, Paramecium = TEAL slipper with a fringe of hairs, green alga = GREEN ball, red blood cell = RED disc pressed in on both faces, bacterium = AMBER short rod, cork boxes = TAN hollow squares. A 'picture' of a cell is a white rounded card holding that cell's icon, with its picture size printed under it. A microscope view is a white circle with a black rim. Any diagram not computed from the lesson's numbers carries a small corner label 'schematic'. A TIMELINE runs along the bottom of the screen, labelled 1665, 1676, about 1840, 1850s (evenly spaced, schematic). A panel on the right lists the cell theory's three parts as three grey, unlit lines. Title card 'A Theory Built in Steps' fades in.

scenes.tts: You now know the three parts of the cell theory. But how did people come to know them? Seeing cells was only the first step. It started with a slice of cork.
scenes.visual: The right panel shows the cell theory's three parts as grey, unlit lines. A large question mark appears beside a row of cartoon living things: a tree, a dog, a mushroom, a drop of water. The size ladder with the BLUE eye line sits small in the left corner.
scenes.narration: You now know the three parts of the cell theory. But how did people come to know them? Seeing cells was only the first step. It started with a slice of cork.

scenes.tts: In sixteen sixty-five, Robert Hooke published a book of drawings made with his microscope. He cut a very thin slice of cork and shone light on it through a lens.
scenes.caption: In 1665, Robert Hooke published a book of drawings made with his microscope. He cut a very thin slice of cork and shone light on it through a lens.
scenes.visual: The timeline marker lights at '1665'. A cartoon of a tree's bark peels away to a cork stopper; a knife shaves a paper-thin slice. The slice lies on a black plate under a simple cartoon microscope while a beam of light shines through a lens onto it.
scenes.narration: In 1665, Robert Hooke published a book of drawings made with his microscope. He cut a very thin slice of cork and shone light on it through a lens.

scenes.tts: He saw tiny spaces with thin walls between them, like a honeycomb. He called them cells. Under his lens, the boxes crossed the eye line.
scenes.visual: Inside a microscope circle, rows of TAN hollow boxes appear, side by side like a honeycomb. On the ladder, a TAN box card slides up from below the BLUE line and crosses it (schematic). A hand-lettered label 'cells' appears over the boxes.
scenes.narration: He saw tiny spaces with thin walls between them, like a honeycomb. He called them cells. Under his lens, the boxes crossed the eye line.

scenes.tts: Cork comes from the bark of a tree. Look closely at the empty boxes. Were Hooke's boxes living cells, or something else?
scenes.visual: The TAN boxes sit in the circle, empty and still. A question mark and the words 'Pause and predict' appear.
scenes.narration: Cork comes from the bark of a tree. Look closely at the empty boxes. Were Hooke's boxes living cells, or something else?

scenes.visual: Hold on the empty TAN boxes; the question mark pulses; a thin countdown bar shrinks along the bottom.

scenes.tts: Something else. The cork cells were dead. Only their walls were left, so Hooke saw the outside of cells, not the living parts inside them.
scenes.visual: The TAN boxes stay as outlines only. A ghostly living cell fades in inside one box, then fades out, leaving the empty wall. Labels: 'dead cells', 'walls only'.
scenes.narration: Something else. The cork cells were dead. Only their walls were left, so Hooke saw the outside of cells, not the living parts inside them.

scenes.tts: In a letter dated sixteen seventy-six, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek described drops of water. He used small microscopes with a single tiny lens. Water from his well looked clear, yet he reported many tiny living things in it.
scenes.caption: In a letter dated 1676, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek described drops of water. He used small microscopes with a single tiny lens. Water from his well looked clear, yet he reported many tiny living things in it.
scenes.visual: The timeline marker moves to '1676'. A cartoon hand holds a tiny flat brass microscope with one bead-sized lens up to an eye. A drop of clear well water appears; inside a microscope circle, small TEAL and GREEN shapes swim and turn.
scenes.narration: In a letter dated 1676, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek described drops of water. He used small microscopes with a single tiny lens. Water from his well looked clear, yet he reported many tiny living things in it.

scenes.tts: He checked one dish of rainwater again and again. At first he found nothing alive in it. Then one day he saw a few tiny creatures, and the next day more.
scenes.visual: A shallow dish of rainwater with a calendar beside it; pages flip. The microscope circle stays empty for several flips, each marked 'nothing'. Then a page reads '30 May': two small swimmers appear. Next page: several more.
scenes.narration: He checked one dish of rainwater again and again. At first he found nothing alive in it. Then one day he saw a few tiny creatures, and the next day more.

scenes.tts: When a view was not clear, he said so and did not count it. His careful records showed that seeing nothing is not the same as nothing being there.
scenes.visual: A blurry microscope circle gets a hand-drawn tick box marked 'unclear: not counted'. Then two cards side by side: 'I saw nothing' and 'nothing is there', with a large not-equal sign between them.
scenes.narration: When a view was not clear, he said so and did not count it. His careful records showed that seeing nothing is not the same as nothing being there.

scenes.tts: Microscopes kept getting better. By about eighteen forty, scientists had looked at many plants and animals, and found cells in them. That was strong evidence for the first part of the theory.
scenes.caption: Microscopes kept getting better. By about 1840, scientists had looked at many plants and animals, and found cells in them. That was strong evidence for the first part of the theory.
scenes.visual: The timeline marker moves to 'about 1840'. A leaf and a slice of animal tissue each open into a microscope circle full of boxes or rounded cells. In the right panel, line 1 begins to glow: 'All living things are made of one or more cells.'
scenes.narration: Microscopes kept getting better. By about 1840, scientists had looked at many plants and animals, and found cells in them. That was strong evidence for the first part of the theory.

scenes.tts: But where do new cells come from? At first, some scientists thought new cells formed out of a clear fluid, a bit like growing crystals. Then a new cell would need no parent cell at all. That idea had to be tested by looking harder.
scenes.visual: A beaker of clear fluid; small cell shapes seem to grow out of it like crystals forming, labelled 'old idea'. The panel's line 3 stays grey.
scenes.narration: But where do new cells come from? At first, some scientists thought new cells formed out of a clear fluid, a bit like growing crystals. Then a new cell would need no parent cell at all. That idea had to be tested by looking harder.

scenes.tts: More observations, including work published in the eighteen fifties, showed that new cells form when a cell divides. One cell becomes two. The theory dropped the wrong idea and kept the rest.
scenes.caption: More observations, including work published in the 1850s, showed that new cells form when a cell divides. One cell becomes two. The theory dropped the wrong idea and kept the rest.
scenes.visual: The timeline marker moves to '1850s'. A large X crosses out the beaker of clear fluid. Beside it, one round cell pinches in the middle and splits into two. In the right panel, line 3 lights up: 'All cells come from cells that already exist.'
scenes.narration: More observations, including work published in the 1850s, showed that new cells form when a cell divides. One cell becomes two. The theory dropped the wrong idea and kept the rest.

scenes.tts: The three parts did not arrive all at once. Many steps came after a better tool or a more careful look. Each one added evidence, and the cell theory grew from it.
scenes.visual: The whole timeline glows, each step with a small icon: cork boxes, rainwater dish, leaf and tissue, dividing cell. All three lines of the theory are now lit in the right panel, including line 2, 'The cell is the basic unit of life'. The size ladder with the BLUE eye line stays in the corner.
scenes.narration: The three parts did not arrive all at once. Many steps came after a better tool or a more careful look. Each one added evidence, and the cell theory grew from it.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex, the hexagon mascot, beside a dividing cell. Take-home line: 'Better microscopes gave evidence, and the cell theory grew and changed.'
